description: Born in the cotton fields of Mississippi, the blues invented the 12-bar grid and fed jazz, rock, soul, and hip-hop.

hero.hook: One cry in the cotton fields, and all modern music has a root.

blocks.text: The blues is not just a genre. It is the mold from which much of Western popular music of the 20th century was cast. It grew out of the poverty of the **Mississippi** cotton fields at the end of the 19th century, as resistance and as expression for African Americans.
From jazz to rock and roll, from soul to hip-hop, its structures and its feeling still run through our ears. To understand the blues is to go back to the source of a cry turned into art.

Between **1870** and **1890**, in the [[Deep South]] of segregation and sharecropper poverty, the blues drew African oral traditions together. The [[field hollers]], lone cries thrown across the fields, and the [[work songs]], steady chants that kept the labor in time, met the [[spirituals]], religious songs that sometimes carried a message of freedom.

The great innovation was the [[12-bar structure]], a three-chord grid that serves as the canvas for improvisation. The [[blue notes]], bent notes, imitate the pain in a voice. The guitar, often played with a [[bottleneck]], a glass or metal tube slid along the strings, answers the singer.
In the lyrics, the word “rider” often stood in for a lover, a way to sing about taboo subjects in front of an audience that would not catch on.

The **Mississippi Delta**, between Memphis and Vicksburg, is the cradle of **Delta blues**, the rawest form of the genre. **Robert Johnson** (**1911**-**1938**) is the wandering musician made flesh: only **29** recordings, and an immense influence. His [[fingerpicking]] treats the guitar like a miniature orchestra.

blocks.caption: The Mississippi Delta: cradle of the rural blues
Robert Johnson: 29 tracks, an eternal legend

blocks.text: Legend says he sold his soul to the devil at a [[crossroads]] in exchange for his gift. The blues was often called “the devil's music” back then, set against the songs of the church. Johnson died young, poisoned. *Cross Road Blues* and *Sweet Home Chicago* became standards.
He recorded facing the wall in a San Antonio hotel, not out of shyness, but to use the acoustics of the room.

sections.title: Robert Johnson and the myth of the Delta

blocks.text: In the **1940s**, the Great Migration carried millions of African Americans to the industrial North. In **Chicago**, the blues plugged in to cut through the noise of the factories. **Muddy Waters** and **Howlin' Wolf** made electric guitar, bass, and drums the new standard.

blocks.caption: Muddy Waters in Chicago: the blues wired to the current

blocks.text: That electrification led straight to rock and roll. **Chuck Berry** and **Bo Diddley** sped up the tempo. In the 1960s, the **Rolling Stones**, named after a Muddy Waters song, and **Led Zeppelin** sold those roots back to white audiences, often without the original creators making a fortune from it.
Muddy Waters was “discovered” by the musicologist Alan Lomax while he was still driving a tractor on a cotton plantation.

Jazz borrowed its structures and its improvisation. Soul and R&B kept its gut-level voice. Hip-hop recycles its legacy through the [[sampling]] of old vinyl. **B.B. King** made the melodic guitar solo popular. More than a historical style, the blues remains a language for lost love, injustice, and hope.

blocks.text: Born from the suffering of Black communities in Mississippi, the blues gave the world the 12-bar grid. By way of Chicago it also gave us rock, and much more besides.
